a: I begin my work with the year
t: How the Bible dates a year
p: Tacitus dates by the Roman consuls. Luke dates John's call by the emperor and the local rulers.
b: Tacitus starts his book with the year's two consuls. The Gospels date events by rulers too, but not by consuls. Luke starts John the Baptist's work like this: "It was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule. Pontius Pilate was governing Judea" (Luke 3:1). Agrees: both anchor a story to men in power so readers can place it in world history. Differs: Luke counts years from the emperor's rule and then names the local governor and tetrarchs, because his readers lived under them. Tacitus writes for readers in the capital, where the consuls named the year.

a: consul for the second time, with Titus Vinius as his colleague
t: The year of Galba and Vinius
p: A Roman year had the names of two consuls. This one was AD 69, and neither man lived to see the end of January.
b: Two consuls were chosen each year, and Romans named the year after them (Wikipedia, Roman consul). Galba's second consulship and Vinius's gave this year its name. Both were dead by 15 January (1:41-42). Tacitus calls it a year "that was the last for them and nearly the last for the state" (1:11). The year is AD 69, as the Year of the Four Emperors page dates it. Josephus calls the whole confusion "sedition and civil war" that reached Italy as well as Judea (Jewish War 4.9.9).

a: The earlier 820 years since Rome was founded
p: Tacitus counts the 820 years since Rome's founding that many writers had already told.
b: The Latin is post conditam urbem octingentos et viginti prioris aevi annos multi auctores rettulerunt: "many authors have told the 820 years of the earlier age after the city was founded." Romans often dated by the years since the founding, ab urbe condita. By that count AD 1 is year 754 (Wikipedia, Ab urbe condita), so the 820th year falls about AD 67, in Nero's last years, and AD 69 is year 822. That is my arithmetic from Wikipedia's table. The Conversational English Translation reads "The earlier 820 years," and the Latin has prioris aevi on those years. Tacitus's own story begins after them.
orig: post conditam urbem octingentos et viginti prioris aevi annos

a: After the war at Actium
t: Actium and the end of free history
p: Tacitus blames one-man rule for the death of honest history writing.
b: Actium was the sea battle where Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra and became master of Rome. He took the name Augustus (Luke 2:1). Tacitus does not name him here. His claim is that when "all power" went to one man, great writers stopped and the truth was bent by ignorance, flattery or hatred. It is a historian's complaint about his own trade. Proverbs speaks of the same danger from the other side: "a smooth-talking mouth brings about a fall" (Proverbs 26:28).

a: flattery carries the ugly charge of servility, while malice looks like honesty
p: Tacitus and Proverbs both treat flattery as a trap.
b: The Latin sets adulatio (flattery) against malignitas (spite). Tacitus says flattery shames a writer, while spite passes for plain speaking, so readers swallow it. Proverbs says the same of the flatterer: "A man who smooth-talks his neighbor / is spreading a net for his steps" (Proverbs 29:5). Jesus warns, "Woe, when all people speak well of you!" (Luke 6:26). Tacitus adds a point the Proverbs do not: the opposite fault, hatred dressed as honesty, is just as untrue.

a: Galba, Otho and Vitellius did me no favors and no harm
p: Tacitus says he can write about these men fairly. Readers have judged his fairness differently.
b: Tacitus's claim: he owes the three emperors of 69 nothing, so he can speak without love or hate. A historian's caution: Wikipedia says his years under Domitian left him "jaded and perhaps ashamed at his own complicity," with a hatred of tyranny that shows in his works. It also notes that Tacitus, Pliny the Younger and Suetonius all wrote about Domitian after his death, and cites the historian Brian Jones, who says the bias of the surviving sources makes Domitian's true character hard to judge. Christian reading: the Bible asks for truth in the one who speaks: "Do not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see clearly" (Exodus 23:8). A writer who owes favors, or hates, sees less.

a: Vespasian started my career
p: Tacitus owes his rank to Vespasian, Titus and Domitian, and says so openly.
b: Wikipedia gives Tacitus's career as quaestor in 81 or 82, praetor in 88 under Domitian, suffect consul in 97 under Nerva and proconsul of Asia in 112 to 113. He was married in 77 or 78 to the daughter of the general Agricola. Here he admits the debt to the Flavian family and still promises fairness to the emperors of 69. Ancient readers knew that history by an insider can be flattering. His honest admission is part of how he asks to be trusted.

a: Titus raised it
p: The men who advanced Tacitus are the men who ended the war in Judea.
b: Titus, son of Vespasian, finished the Jewish war: Wikipedia dates the capture of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Second Temple to AD 70. Jesus had said of the city, "they will not leave stone on stone within you" (Luke 19:44), and of the Temple, "here not one stone will be left on a stone" (Matthew 24:2). Same person? Very likely: Tacitus's Vespasian and Titus, Josephus's commanders (Jewish War 3.1.1-3; 4.9.2) and the Flavian generals who ended the war are the same two men, by name, office and place. This Titus is not Paul's coworker Titus (Galatians 2:1).

a: the divine Nerva and the rule of Trajan
p: Tacitus planned to write about Nerva and Trajan in his old age.
b: Domitian was murdered on 18 September 96, and Nerva succeeded him the same day (Wikipedia, Domitian). Suetonius says Domitian was slain on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October (Domitian 17.3), which is 18 September. Tacitus calls Nerva "divine" (divus), the word he also uses for the dead Augustus and the dead Julius (1:15, 1:42), so he writes as if Nerva has died. Wikipedia says the Histories were thought to run to Domitian's death in 96, and that the Annals came later. The book we have breaks off in the middle of a sentence in Book 5 (5:26). The promised age of Nerva and Trajan is not in it.

a: a rare and happy time when you can think what you like and say what you think
t: Free speech in Rome and in Acts
p: Tacitus longs for free speech. Acts ends with Paul in Rome, speaking freely.
b: The Latin is ubi sentire quae velis et quae sentias dicere licet. Tacitus treats such freedom as rare. Acts ends in Rome with Paul "proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching the things about the Lord Jesus Christ, with complete freedom to speak, and no one stopped him" (Acts 28:31). Background link: the two are far apart in kind and in date. Paul's freedom is the freedom of a prisoner under guard (Acts 28:16). Peter and John said, "We cannot keep from telling the things we saw and heard" (Acts 4:20).

a: Four emperors were killed by the sword
p: Tacitus does not name the four in this sentence.
b: Tacitus says four emperors were killed by the sword and that three civil wars were fought. The Latin, quattuor principes ferro interempti and trina bella civilia, does not name the four or the wars, and does not say they all fall in one year. Galba, Otho and Vitellius all died in AD 69 (Galba killed, 1:41; Wikipedia on Otho and on Vitellius). Which fourth he means is not given in the sentence.

a: the Parthians very nearly went to war, fooled by a fake Nero
p: A man pretending to be Nero stirred up trouble in the East. Revelation's beast may echo the rumor.
b: Nero died in AD 68, but rumors said he was alive in the East. The site's note on Revelation 13:3 says at least three impostors appeared. Revelation says of the beast, "One of its heads looked as if it had been slaughtered to death, but its death wound was healed" (Revelation 13:3). Some readers link that verse to the Nero legend. Link strength: debated. John does not name Nero, and futurists read the verse of a coming ruler. Parthians are listed among those in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9).

a: Cities on the richest coast of Campania were swallowed up or buried
p: Tacitus does not say what swallowed these cities.
b: Campania is the coast around the Bay of Naples. Tacitus wrote after AD 79, when Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum (Wikipedia, Titus), and "buried" fits that. He does not name the mountain. Suetonius says Titus named commissioners from among the ex-consuls for the relief of Campania and used the property of those who died with no heirs for "the buried cities" (Titus 8.4). The Bible's stories of disaster, such as Sodom, are told as acts of God (Genesis 19:24-25); Tacitus lists the same kind of event without a cause.

a: Rome was ravaged by fires, its oldest temples were burned down
p: Tacitus may have two fires in mind: Nero's fire and the burning of the Capitol.
b: Rome had a great fire in AD 64 under Nero. The site's topic on Nero says he blamed Christians for it and had many killed, and that tradition says Peter and Paul died under him. Tacitus does not give the year here. The next clause points to the burning of the Capitol in December 69 (told in Book 3). The Jerusalem Temple was destroyed in AD 70 (Wikipedia, Titus), so within about a year Rome's holiest hill and the Jews' holiest house both burned.

a: the Capitol itself was set on fire by the hands of citizens
p: The temple of Jupiter on the Capitol burned in the civil war. Who started the fire is disputed.
b: The Capitol was the hill with Rome's greatest temple, Jupiter's. Who set the fire is disputed. In Book 3 Tacitus has Vitellius's men storm the hill, where Flavius Sabinus and his party were besieged, and says it is uncertain whether the attackers threw the lighted brands on to the roofs or whether, as "the more general account" has it, the besieged did so to drive the attackers back (3:71, Church and Brodribb). Wikipedia's page on the Year of the Four Emperors says Vespasian's men "burned down the temple of Jupiter" in seizing the capital, and its page on Domitian says Vitellianists burst onto the Capitol on 19 December. Domitian was on the hill and got away dressed in a linen robe among the temple's attendants (Tacitus 3:74). In the preface Tacitus names the deed as done "by the hands of citizens" (1:2).

a: The sea was full of exiles
p: Rome sent exiles to islands. John wrote Revelation on Patmos.
b: Rome punished important people by sending them to an island. John says, "I was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 1:9). Link strength: weak. John does not say he was exiled by Rome, and Tacitus is speaking of nobles under Nero and other emperors, not of Christians. It shows why a reader of that day would picture an island as a place of banishment.

a: The informers' rewards were as hated as their crimes.
p: Informers (delatores) won money by accusing others. John the Baptist told soldiers not to do it.
b: Tacitus says informers took priesthoods and consulships as spoils (1:2). John the Baptist told soldiers, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges" (Luke 3:14). Agrees: both see false accusation for gain as wrong. The law of Moses has an older rule against it: "Keep far from a false charge" (Exodus 23:7).

a: Slaves were bribed against their masters and freedmen against their patrons, and men who had no enemy were ruined by their friends.
p: Tacitus's picture of betrayal by one's own household has Bible echoes.
b: A freedman was a former slave, and a patron was the man who had freed him. Tacitus says informers' pressure broke these bonds. The Bible knows the same grief. "Even the man I was at peace with, the one I trusted, / who ate my bread, / has raised his heel high against me" (Psalm 41:9). Jesus warns, "One brother will hand another over to be killed" (Matthew 10:21). Link strength: shared human pattern, not a source.

a: The work I'm starting is rich in disasters
t: Two lists of signs, two verdicts
p: Claude's theory: Tacitus and Jesus list similar signs in the same decades and judge them differently.
b: My theory. Tacitus lists wars, revolts, disasters and signs in sky and earth (1:2-3). Jesus lists wars, earthquakes, famines and "great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:9-11) and calls such things "the start of the labor pains" (Mark 13:8). Both lists describe the first-century world, but they draw opposite lessons. Tacitus concludes that "the gods care nothing for our safety, only for punishing us" (1:3). Jesus says the pains lead to birth and the end "is not here yet" (Matthew 24:6). This is my reading of the contrast, not a claim that either man knew the other's words. The site's topic on the Olivet discourse sets out how that passage is read. A web search on 3 November 2026 found no published comparison of Tacitus's list with Jesus' list, so the comparison here is mine.

a: Famous men faced their last hours bravely
p: Tacitus honors those who died well. Acts tells of a death with a different prayer.
b: Tacitus says the age still produced good deaths "matched ... the praised deaths of the ancients." Romans prized a calm, even defiant end. Acts tells of Stephen, stoned while he prayed: "Lord Jesus, welcome my spirit" and "Lord, do not count this sin against them!" (Acts 7:59-60). Differs: the Roman hero shows his own courage and contempt for the killer; Stephen asks forgiveness for the killers. The site's topic on martyrs follows this thread.

a: signs in the sky and on the earth, warnings from thunder
p: Tacitus lists omens. Jesus also spoke of signs, but about the end.
b: Tacitus, like most Romans, took thunder and strange sights as messages from the gods. Jesus said, "There will be terrors, and great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:11), and also, "The signs of the times, though, you cannot read" (Matthew 16:3). Deuteronomy bans "anyone who practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens or works sorcery" (Deuteronomy 18:10). Differs: in the Bible God warns openly through prophets, while omen-reading is forbidden.

a: the gods care nothing for our safety, only for punishing us
p: Tacitus says the gods only punish. The Bible says God cares and is patient.
b: The Latin, non esse curae deis securitatem nostram, esse ultionem, says that the gods care nothing for our safety, only for revenge. The Bible answers it directly. Jesus says of the sparrow, "not one of them falls to the ground without your Father," and "You matter more than a great many sparrows" (Matthew 10:29, 31). God says, "I take no pleasure in the death of a wicked man" (Ezekiel 33:11), and "he bears patiently with you. He does not want any to be lost" (2 Peter 3:9). Answers: judgment is real in the Bible, but it is never the whole of how God cares.
orig: non esse curae deis securitatem nostram, esse ultionem

a: which are mostly chance
p: Tacitus says events are mostly chance. Ecclesiastes agrees that things look that way. Proverbs says otherwise.
b: The Latin is casus eventusque rerum, qui plerumque fortuiti sunt: the turns of events are mostly fortuiti, "by chance." Ecclesiastes sees the same: "the race does not belong to the swift... For time and chance meet them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Proverbs gives the other half: "People throw the lot into the lap, / but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Tacitus looks for reasons and causes beneath the chance, which is what he promises next.
orig: casus eventusque rerum, qui plerumque fortuiti sunt

a: The secret of the empire was out: an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome.
p: Galba was made emperor in Spain, and Vespasian later in Egypt.
b: The Latin evulgato imperii arcano posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri says that an emperor could be made away from Rome. Galba was acclaimed in Spain (Wikipedia, Galba). The Rhine legions made Vitellius (1:56-57). Vespasian was proclaimed at Alexandria on 1 July 69 (Wikipedia, Vespasian). Daniel says God "removes kings and he sets kings up" (Daniel 2:21); Tacitus sees armies doing it. Paul says, "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1), and he wrote to Rome in these decades.
orig: evulgato imperii arcano posse principem alibi quam Romae fieri

a: The leading Roman Knights
p: The Knights were Rome's wealthy class below the senators.
b: Wikipedia, Equites, says a Roman Knight (eques) was entitled to wear a gold ring, and that Augustus' law let any Roman citizen assessed at a property of 100,000 denarii use the title and wear the ring. Wikipedia, Denarius, gives 25 denarii as equal to 100 sestertii, so a denarius was four sesterces and 100,000 denarii is 400,000 sesterces; the conversion is my arithmetic. Offices open to Knights included command of the Praetorian Guard, the prefecture of Egypt and procurators of imperial provinces. Tacitus names them again at 1:11 and 1:13. They sit between the Senate and the people in his list of who rejoiced at Nero's fall.

a: the dependents and freed slaves of condemned and exiled men
p: Tacitus's "freed slaves" are a class the Book of Acts also names.
b: A freed slave (libertus) was a former slave. Acts names "the synagogue called the Freedmen's" in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). Link strength: background. The word shows that freed people formed a recognized group in Roman life. Whether the Jerusalem freedmen were Jews freed in the Roman world is not stated in Acts.

a: The city's soldiers
t: The Praetorian Guard enters the story
p: "The city's soldiers" means the Praetorian Guard and its fellow units at Rome.
b: The Latin miles urbanus means the troops stationed in the capital. The Praetorian Guard was the emperor's bodyguard: Wikipedia says Augustus kept it, that Claudius was the first emperor the Guard proclaimed in AD 41, and that each new emperor was expected to pay a donative. Tacitus says these men had been "bound by their oath to the Caesars." They turn against Nero, then against Galba, then are bought by Otho. The Guard is his hinge for the year. Paul meets the same word in another form, praitorion (Philippians 1:13). Look at the note on that word at verse 13 of this book, below.

a: the bonus promised in Galba's name wasn't being paid
p: Soldiers wanted a bonus. John the Baptist told soldiers to make do with their pay.
b: Wikipedia explains that a donative was a gift of money soldiers expected from a new emperor. The Praetorians had been promised one in Galba's name by Nymphidius, and never got it. Soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do, and he answered, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges. Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14). Answers: John's rule would have undone the whole system of bonuses and exemption fees that Tacitus describes (1:46).

a: Nymphidius Sabinus
p: Plutarch tells Nymphidius's whole story. Tacitus has only a sentence.
b: Tacitus passes over Nymphidius in one sentence (1:5). Plutarch gives him chapters: Nymphidius talked the soldiers into proclaiming Galba with promises of large gifts, grasped at power in Rome, and was cut down in a soldier's hut by the troops (Plutarch, Galba 2, 8, 13-15). Suetonius says Galba overthrew Nymphidius, prefect of the Guard, after he plotted against him (Galba 11). Link strength: strong. All three tell the same event; Plutarch and Suetonius add detail Tacitus leaves out.

a: I pick my soldiers, I don't buy them.
t: "I pick my soldiers, I don't buy them"
p: Galba's saying turns on one Latin word play. Suetonius gives the same saying.
b: The Latin is legi a se militem, non emi: a soldier is "picked" (legere), not "bought" (emere). Suetonius gives it too: it was Galba's habit to "levy troops, not buy them" (Galba 16.1), and notes the unpaid bonus angered the soldiers across the empire. Tacitus calls it "noble for the state but dangerous for himself." The line also fits Galba's stinginess, which Tacitus returns to at 1:18.
orig: legi a se militem, non emi

a: fourteen years under Nero
p: Nero ruled from AD 54 to 68.
b: The site's topic on Nero gives his rule as AD 54 to 68, fourteen years, which matches Tacitus. Acts never names Nero, only "Caesar" (Acts 25:11-12), and Paul's greeting from "Caesar's household" comes from Rome (Philippians 4:22).

a: Titus Vinius and Cornelius Laco
p: Vinius and Laco were Galba's chief men.
b: Tacitus will say at 1:13 that Vinius was consul and Laco was prefect of the Praetorian Guard. He treats the two as the real power behind an old emperor. Plutarch agrees that Galba put himself into the hands of Vinius, Laco and their freedmen (Galba 29).

a: Both died without a hearing or a defense, as if they were innocent men.
p: Tacitus condemns killing men unheard. Rome's own custom, as Festus tells it, required a hearing.
b: Romans of the day held that a man should face his accusers. Festus said so to King Agrippa: "Romans do not have a custom of making a gift of any man before the accused has his accusers in front of him, face to face, and gets room to defend himself against the charge" (Acts 25:16). A related right comes up when Paul, about to be whipped, asks whether the law lets them whip a Roman "and one who has not been found guilty" (Acts 22:25). Agrees: the ideal. Tacitus shows how far Galba's reign fell short of it.

a: the one Nero had raised from the fleet
p: Nero raised a legion from sailors. Galba later killed many of them.
b: The Year of the Four Emperors page says the legion I Adiutrix was created by Nero from naval sailors. Tacitus does not name the legion here, so the sailors he mentions are probably that legion. At 1:31 he says Galba had them cut down the moment he entered the city, and at 1:37 and 1:87 he gives their story from Otho's side. Wikipedia's page on decimation adds that Galba decimated a unit that refused to be sent back to naval service.

a: Clodius Macer and Fonteius Capito
p: Macer in Africa and Capito in Germany were killed. Tacitus gives two views of Capito.
b: Tacitus says Macer was plainly stirring up trouble in Africa and the procurator Trebonius Garutianus killed him on Galba's order. Capito's guilt is disputed: some thought he never meant revolt and that his legates, Cornelius Aquinus and Fabius Valens, invented the charge. Here Tacitus shows his method: he reports two stories, says plainly which he thinks weaker, and leaves the question open. Valens later pushes Vitellius into revolt (1:52).

a: Cluvius Rufus, a skilled speaker
p: Tacitus names the governor of Spain, who is also one of Tacitus's own sources.
b: Wikipedia's page on Tacitus lists Cluvius Rufus, Fabius Rusticus and Pliny the Elder as authorities Tacitus cites by name. Here Cluvius Rufus appears as a character: governor of Spain, a skilled speaker, but with no experience of war. He is praised in an edict at 1:76. A historian writing about a man who is also one of his sources is a reason to read the portrait with care.

a: Among the provinces, Spain
t: Spain in Tacitus and in Romans
p: Spain comes up again and again in Book 1. Paul hoped to go there.
b: Tacitus puts Spain first among the provinces: Cluvius Rufus governed it (1:8), Otho had been governor of Lusitania (1:13, 1:21), and in 1:76 Spain first swears to Otho and then turns to Vitellius. Paul told the Romans of a plan to visit it: "when I make my trip to Spain. I hope to see you on my way through" (Romans 15:24). Link strength: place only. Tacitus writes of governors and armies in AD 69, Paul of a mission plan, and neither mentions the other.

a: the recent gift of Roman citizenship
p: Galba and Otho gave citizenship to whole peoples. In Acts, citizenship is either born into or bought.
b: Tacitus says Galba tied the Gauls to him by "the recent gift of Roman citizenship." At 1:78 Otho gives it to all the Lingones. In Acts the commander in Jerusalem said, "It cost me a great deal of money to acquire this citizenship." Paul replied, "I, though, was born to it" (Acts 22:28). Agrees: citizenship was valued and could be granted or bought. Paul's "born to it" is also why the magistrates at Philippi were frightened (Acts 16:38).

a: the promise of lighter tribute in the future
p: The Gauls were promised lighter tribute. The Gospels and Paul speak about paying tribute to Rome.
b: "Tribute" is the tax a province paid to Rome. Jesus was asked, "Is it permitted to pay the head tax to Caesar, or not?" and answered, "pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (Matthew 22:17, 21). Paul wrote, "If it is the tax, pay the tax" (Romans 13:7). Link strength: background. Tacitus shows tribute as a political tool a ruler can lighten to buy loyalty.

a: consular rank
p: A commander of "consular rank" had already been consul.
b: Wikipedia's page on consuls says that under the emperors only former consuls could serve as "consular legates," generals who governed the largest provinces. Tacitus complains that Lower Germany went so long without such a man. The system Tacitus describes, with senators as legates and Knights as procurators, is the same one in which the New Testament's governors served (Luke 3:1; Acts 23:24).

a: Aulus Vitellius arrived by Galba's appointment
p: Vitellius owed his command to his father's name.
b: Tacitus says his father had been censor and three times consul, which "seemed to be enough." Wikipedia names the father as Lucius Vitellius. Wikipedia also says Galba chose him for Lower Germany at the end of 68, which the page calls a surprise. Tacitus tells the choice as a sign of how thin Galba's judgment was.

a: Illyricum was quiet too
p: Paul says he preached as far as Illyricum.
b: Illyricum was the Roman land along the Adriatic coast, east of Italy. Paul wrote to the Romans, "from Jerusalem and around in a circle as far as Illyricum, I have completed the preaching of the good news of Christ" (Romans 15:19). Link strength: place only. Tacitus is writing about legions in AD 69, Paul about mission earlier. It shows the same frontier roads in two very different stories.

a: Licinius Mucianus governed Syria and its four legions
p: Syria was Rome's key eastern province, and the Bible names its governors too.
b: Tacitus gives Syria's governor four legions, and Wikipedia's page on Vespasian says Mucianus commanded three, so the sources differ. Either way it was a very large command. Luke dates the registration "while Quirinius governed Syria" (Luke 2:2). Antioch in Syria is where the disciples were first called Christians. Wikipedia says Mucianus urged Vespasian in May 69 to challenge Vitellius and ran Rome for a time afterward. Same person? Mucianus is not named in the Bible. The link is the office and the province.

a: Flavius Vespasian was running the war in Judea
p: Tacitus and Josephus both say Nero chose Vespasian to put down the Jewish revolt.
b: Josephus: Nero found "no one but Vespasian equal to the task" and sent him to Syria (Jewish War 3.1.2-3). Tacitus's phrase is "Nero had chosen him." This is the war that ended with Jerusalem's fall. Jesus had said, "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). Josephus says Vespasian put off his expedition after Nero died and waited for Galba's orders (Jewish War 4.9.2); Tacitus does not say this in Book 1. Same person? Very likely: Tacitus's and Josephus's Vespasian is one man, the future emperor.

a: with three legions
p: Tacitus says three legions. Josephus and Wikipedia help count them.
b: Wikipedia says Vespasian had two legions, eight cavalry squadrons and ten auxiliary cohorts when Nero sent him, and that Titus brought a third. Josephus says Vespasian sent Titus from Greece to Alexandria "to bring back with him from thence the fifth and the tenth legions" (Jewish War 3.1.3). Tacitus's three legions fit that count. A legion was about 5,000 men (Wikipedia).

a: He had even sent his son Titus to pay his respects and show his loyalty
t: Titus and King Agrippa on the way to Galba
p: Josephus adds that King Agrippa sailed with Titus. He is the Agrippa who met Paul.
b: Josephus: Vespasian "sent his son Titus to him, to salute him, and to receive his commands about the Jews. Upon the very same errand did king Agrippa sail along with Titus." In the winter, off the coast of Achaia, they heard that Galba was dead after reigning seven months and as many days; Agrippa went on to Rome, and Titus sailed back to his father (Jewish War 4.9.2). Tacitus tells the turning back in Book 2: Titus learned of Galba's death at Corinth, weighed the risks, and some said he went back for love of Queen Berenice (2:1-2). The two give different reasons; Josephus says "by a Divine impulse." Same person as in Acts? Very likely. The site's topic on the Herod family says Agrippa II "heard Paul (Acts 25-26)," and Acts 25:13 has "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice."

a: the omens and the oracles that marked out the throne for Vespasian and his sons
p: Several ancient writers said a prophecy pointed to Vespasian. The Bible's promised king points elsewhere.
b: Wikipedia reports three accounts: Josephus read a scriptural prophecy of a man from the Jewish nation ruling the world as meaning Vespasian; Suetonius wrote of a widespread Eastern prophecy that rulers of the world would come from Judea; Tacitus agreed the prophecy concerned Vespasian and Titus but said ordinary people misread it through ambition. Christian reading: the Bible's own promise of a coming king is read by Christians as fulfilled in Jesus, "the newborn king of the Jews" (Matthew 2:2). Josephus applied the hope to the Roman general instead.

a: Roman Knights have governed Egypt in place of kings
p: Augustus had Egypt ruled by a Knight, not a senator.
b: Wikipedia calls the prefecture of Egypt the most prestigious post open to Roman Knights. Tacitus gives the reason: Egypt was hard to reach, rich in grain and restless, so it was thought best to keep it close at home under the emperor's own men. Egypt in the Bible is both refuge and prison (Matthew 2:13; Exodus 1-14).

a: rich in grain
p: Tacitus calls Egypt rich in grain. Acts has a ship from Alexandria carrying wheat.
b: Luke writes of Paul's voyage: "the centurion came across a ship out of Alexandria bound for Italy, and he moved us onto it" (Acts 27:6). When the storm came, "they made the ship lighter by dumping the wheat into the sea" (Acts 27:38). So the ship was a grain carrier, which fits Tacitus's point that Egypt was rich in grain and kept in the emperor's hands. Apollos of Alexandria also appears in Acts (Acts 18:24).

a: restless and excitable through superstition and wildness
p: A restless Egypt appears in the commander's question to Paul.
b: When the commander in Jerusalem arrested Paul, he asked, "So you are not that Egyptian, the one who started an uprising a while back and took the four thousand men of the Sicarii out to the wilderness?" (Acts 21:38). Link strength: background only. Tacitus is giving a Roman's harsh view of the Egyptian people. Acts mentions one Egyptian rebel, who is not the subject here. Judge the Roman view fairly: it is one writer's prejudice, not evidence.

a: Tiberius Alexander, a native of the country
p: Josephus tells more about this man, including his crucifixion of the sons of Judas the Galilean.
b: Tiberius Alexander was born into a Jewish family. Josephus says he was the son of Alexander the alabarch of Alexandria and "did not continue in the religion of his country." He followed Cuspius Fadus as procurator of Judea (Josephus, Jewish War 2.11.6; Antiquities 20.5.2), and ordered James and Simon, sons of Judas of Galilee, to be crucified. Acts mentions this Judas: "Judas the Galilean appeared at the time of the registration" (Acts 5:37; compare Luke 2:2). In Alexandria he held back a Jewish riot (Jewish War 2.18.7) and in 69 had the legions swear to Vespasian (Jewish War 4.10.6). Same person? Very likely: Tacitus's and Josephus's Tiberius Alexander share name, province and role.

a: a letter came from the procurator Pompeius Propinquus in Belgica
p: A provincial procurator writes to Galba to warn him. He is killed later (1:58).
b: Wikipedia explains a procurator was an official in charge of a province's money, reporting to the emperor. Pompeius Propinquus warns Galba of the mutiny on the Rhine, then is killed by Vitellius's men (1:58). Paul had dealings with procurators too: Felix (Acts 23:24) and Festus (Acts 25:11-12).

a: Cornelius Laco, the prefect of the Praetorian Guard
p: Laco commanded the Guard and was one of Galba's two chief men.
b: The Praetorian prefect was the Guard's commander (Wikipedia). Laco kept his post through Galba's reign, blocked the plan to send Piso to the Rhine (1:19) and waved off warnings of Otho's plot (1:26). He is killed at 1:46. Wikipedia says from Vespasian on the prefect was an equestrian.

a: Praetorian Guard
p: Paul's chains became known to the "praetorium." The Guard is one reading.
b: Paul wrote from custody, "My chains are now seen for what they are, chains for Christ, by the whole praetorium and by everyone else" (Philippians 1:13). The Greek praitorion is a Latin loanword. In the Gospels it is Pilate's headquarters (Mark 15:16) and in Acts Herod's palace at Caesarea (Acts 23:35). In Rome it may mean the Guard. The site's note on Philippians 1:13 sets out both readings. Philippians 4:22 sends greetings from "those who belong to Caesar's household." Link strength: the word is real; whether Paul means this Guard is open.

a: Icelus, a freed slave of Galba's
t: A freedman who got a knight's rank
p: Icelus was given the gold rings of a Knight and a knightly name.
b: Wikipedia says a Knight wore a gold ring. Galba gave Icelus that honor even though he had been a slave. The Latin has him go by the knightly name Marcianus (Marcianum, 1:13, 1:46), and Plutarch says Icelus brought Galba the news of Nero's death and was given the gold ring and the name Marcianus (Galba 7). Tacitus has him executed in public as a freedman (1:46). The Bible's own list of Caesar's household includes people of low rank (Philippians 4:22).

a: Poppaea Sabina
p: Josephus says Poppaea, Nero's wife, helped the Jewish leaders.
b: The sources tell the Poppaea affair differently. Tacitus has Nero put Poppaea, his favorite mistress, in Otho's care (1:13), and Suetonius says she was turned over to Otho, who pretended marriage with her (Otho 3.1). Wikipedia's page on Otho has her as Otho's wife who took up with Nero. Josephus says a Jewish embassy won a favor from Nero "to gratify Poppea, Nero's wife, who was a religious woman" (Antiquities 20.8.11). Whiston's footnote adds that she may have been a Jewish proselyte. Link strength: contact with Jewish leaders is shown; her faith is a guess. Gentile women drawn to God appear in Acts, such as Cornelius, who "feared God" (Acts 10:2).

a: Piso Licinianus
t: Piso's adoption in Plutarch and Suetonius
p: Plutarch and Suetonius agree Galba adopted Piso in the camp. Plutarch adds the storm.
b: Plutarch: Galba adopted Piso, son of Crassus and Scribonia, instead of Otho or Dolabella, and went to the camp to name him Caesar and heir. Thunder, lightning and rain interrupted the reading of the address, which Plutarch takes as a sign that the gods did not favor it (Galba 23). Suetonius says Galba adopted him before the Praetorian soldiers but gave them no gift, which made it easier for Otho to act "within six days" (Galba 17.1). Link strength: strong. The accounts agree.

a: They say Galba took Piso by the hand and spoke like this
p: Tacitus says "they say" Galba spoke. The words are Tacitus's art.
b: The Latin ferunt means "they say." Tacitus was about thirteen in AD 69 (Wikipedia: born about 56), so he was not in the room. The speech is long and polished. Historical-critical question: how far are the words Tacitus's rather than Galba's? He himself says Otho's speech at 1:90 may have been another man's work. Christian reading: read the speech as Tacitus's own judgment on adoption and empire, put into Galba's mouth. Plutarch reports only that Galba's address was cut short by a storm (Galba 23).

a: If I were a private man adopting you
t: Adoption in Rome and in Paul
p: Roman adoption chose an heir. Paul uses the same word for what God does.
b: Galba names the form of a private adoption, "by the law of the Curiae before the pontiffs" (1:15). As emperor he does it by "the agreement of gods and men." Paul uses the Greek huiothesia, "adoption": "You received the Spirit of adoption as children" (Romans 8:15), "We would receive adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5), "We would be adopted as his children through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:5). The site's topic on adoption says the word comes from Greek and Roman law. Differs: Galba hunts for the best heir. God adopts slaves.

a: by the law of the Curiae before the pontiffs
p: A private adoption took place in a formal ceremony before the priests.
b: The Latin is lege curiata apud pontifices. Galba names it as the way a private man would adopt, "as our custom is," and says his own case is different: he has been called to power "by the agreement of gods and men." The Conversational English Translation keeps the Latin names so the reader can see that a formal procedure lies behind the word "adopt."

a: a descendant of Gnaeus Pompeius and Marcus Crassus
p: Piso descended from Pompey. Pompey was the first Roman to capture Jerusalem.
b: Gnaeus Pompeius is Pompey the Great. The site's topic on Rome says Rome "took Jerusalem under Pompey in 63 BC." Tacitus says in Book 5 that Pompey was "the first Roman to conquer the Jews" (5:9). Same person? Very likely: Gnaeus Pompeius here is the Pompey who took Jerusalem, by name and by the family line Tacitus draws.

a: I follow the example of the divine Augustus
p: Augustus is the emperor in Luke 2:1. Tacitus calls him divine after his death.
b: Luke begins the birth of Jesus: "an order came out from Caesar Augustus: the whole inhabited world was to be registered" (Luke 2:1). Same person? Very likely: Tacitus's "divine Augustus" and Luke's "Caesar Augustus" are the first emperor, the one who won at Actium (1:1). Tacitus calls Augustus "divine" because he is dead; the imperial cult worshipped emperors (see the site's topic). Acts 12:22 shows the same human claim: "It's a god speaking, not a man!"

a: last Tiberius Nero, his stepson
p: Augustus's stepson is the emperor in whose fifteenth year John began preaching.
b: Luke dates John's call: "It was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule" (Luke 3:1). Same person? Very likely. Tacitus's "Tiberius Nero, his stepson" is the Tiberius whom Augustus made his heir, and Luke's Tiberius Caesar is that emperor. Pilate's title in Luke 3:1 is "governing" Judea; Wikipedia says the Pilate Stone shows his title was prefect.

a: Good fortune tests the spirit with sharper stings, because misery can be put up with, but success corrupts us.
p: Galba warns Piso that good fortune is the harder test. Proverbs prays the same.
b: Agur prays, "Do not give me poverty or riches... or else I may be full and deny you, / and say, 'Who is the LORD?'" (Proverbs 30:8-9). Tacitus has Galba say that misery can be borne and prosperity corrupts. Both see riches as a harder test of the soul than want. Piso says it himself in his own speech (1:29).

a: Under Tiberius, Caligula and Claudius we were, so to speak, the inheritance of one family.
p: The emperors of the Julian and Claudian family: the New Testament names three and never names Nero.
b: Luke names Augustus (Luke 2:1) and Tiberius (Luke 3:1). Acts names Claudius twice: Agabus's famine "in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28) and the order that "all the Jews must leave Rome" (Acts 18:2). Caligula is not named. Nero is not named; Acts speaks of "Caesar" (Acts 25:11-12). Same person? Very likely for Tiberius and Claudius; Nero as the Caesar of Acts 25 is very likely by the dates, though the text does not say his name. The Jewish expulsion from Rome under Claudius also touches Tacitus's world.
r: Luke 2:1; Luke 3:1; Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2; Acts 25:11-12; Philippians 4:22

a: In adoption the judgment is free
t: Choosing the best, or choosing the lost
p: Claude's theory: Paul's "adoption" would sound to Roman ears like Galba's, and turn it upside down.
b: My theory. Galba argues that adoption is better than birth because it picks the best man (1:16). Paul writes to the Romans about adoption (Romans 8:15) and says God "decided beforehand that we would be adopted as his children through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:5). Roman readers had seen adoption used to choose a worthy heir. Paul's gospel adopts people who were slaves to fear (Romans 8:15), and it does so because God wanted it, not because they were the best. This is my reading. The site's topic on adoption already says the word comes from Greek and Roman law. A web search on 3 November 2026 found no published comparison of Galba's speech with Paul's word, so the comparison is mine.

a: It was not Vindex with his unarmed province, or I with my one legion, who took him off our necks
p: A revolt in Gaul and a legion in Spain, not armies, ended Nero.
b: Wikipedia says Julius Vindex revolted in Gaul in 68, and that Galba broke with Nero and styled himself "General of the Senate and People of Rome." Galba here says that neither of them, but Nero's own cruelty, brought him down. Josephus's short summary of these years mentions how Nero slew himself and how the war in Gaul ended (Jewish War 4.9.2).

a: You will rule men who can't stand being total slaves and can't handle total freedom.
p: Galba's last line has a New Testament echo about freedom.
b: Peter tells believers, "You are free, yet do not hold your freedom up as a veil to hide wrongdoing. You are free as God's slaves" (1 Peter 2:16). Link strength: background. Tacitus has Galba say a ruler of Rome faces a people who cannot bear servitude or liberty. Peter tells people already under Rome to honor the king (1 Peter 2:17).

a: January 10 was an ugly day
t: The date: the fourth day before the Ides
p: The Latin counts back from the Ides. January 10.
b: The Latin is Quartum idus Ianuarias. Wikipedia explains that Romans counted backward and inclusively from the Kalends (1st), Nones and Ides. In January the Nones fall on the 5th and the Ides on the 13th. The fourth day before the Ides is therefore 10 January.

a: thunder, lightning and threats from the sky were worse than usual
t: Thunder at the adoption in Plutarch
p: Plutarch also has a storm on the day of the adoption.
b: Plutarch says thunder, lightning and rain interrupted the reading of Galba's address, and that this was taken as a sign the adoption was not favored (Galba 23). Tacitus says old custom saw such storms as a reason to break up an assembly. Link strength: strong on the fact of the storm; the interpretation is each writer's. Luke 21:11 speaks of "great signs from the sky" before the end, but about something far greater.

a: as the divine Augustus had done and as soldiers do when one picks a comrade
p: Galba compares the adoption to a soldier choosing a comrade.
b: Galba speaks to the soldiers in their own terms. The oath each soldier took bound him to the emperor and the emperor's family (1:5). So he presents the adoption as a soldier's choice, not a court's. He announces it "as briefly as an emperor does." Suetonius adds that he gave the soldiers no gift (Galba 17.1).

a: In the four days between his adoption and his killing
p: Piso's reign counts differently in different places.
b: Tacitus says four days lay between the adoption (10 January) and the killing (15 January, 1:27): the 11th, 12th, 13th and 14th. Piso says in his speech that it is "the sixth day" since the adoption (1:29), counting both ends. Suetonius says Otho acted "within six days" (Galba 17.1). All three agree once you see how each counts. Tacitus then says Piso was "Caesar for four days" (1:48).

a: Nero had poured out two thousand two hundred million sesterces in gifts
p: A sesterce was a small coin. This sum is thousands of times what it took to be a Knight.
b: Four sesterces made a denarius (Wikipedia, Denarius: 25 denarii equal 100 sestertii). In Jesus' parable a worker agreed on "one denarius for the day's work" (Matthew 20:2). Wikipedia, Equites, gives the property requirement for a Knight under Augustus as 100,000 denarii, which is 400,000 sesterces at that rate. Tacitus's sum is 5,500 times that, or 550 million denarii, which is 550 million days of a laborer's pay at the parable's rate. The conversion and the comparison are my arithmetic; the figure is Tacitus's.

a: Thirty Roman Knights were put in charge of collecting.
p: Galba used Knights, not senators, to take back Nero's gifts.
b: Knights handled money for the emperor as procurators (Wikipedia, Procurator). Tacitus says this was "a new kind of office," made heavy by lobbying and by the numbers. The city filled with lawsuits and auction sales. Soldiers and tax collectors both came to John the Baptist to ask what to do (Luke 3:12-14); the soldiers' answer is quoted at 1:5.

a: some tribunes were dismissed: Antonius Taurus and Antonius Naso from the Praetorian Guard, Aemilius Pacensis from the city cohorts, and Julius Fronto from the watch
t: Three kinds of soldiers in Rome
p: Rome had three bodies of soldiers: the Guard, the city cohorts and the watch.
b: The Praetorian Guard was the emperor's bodyguard. Wikipedia says the Urban Cohorts were the garrison of Rome. The watch (vigiles) was the city's fire brigade and constabulary, commanded by a Knight (Wikipedia, Equites). Tacitus names a tribune from each. Dismissing them one at a time frightened all three bodies instead of calming them.

a: another Lusitania
p: Suetonius says Nero sent Otho to Lusitania and that he governed well.
b: Suetonius: Nero sent Otho to Lusitania under the form of a governorship, because a harsher punishment would have made the affair public (Otho 3.2), and Otho governed with notable moderation (Otho 3.3). Wikipedia gives the date as 58 or 59. Tacitus agrees at 1:13 that Otho "ran the province with kindness." Link strength: strong.

a: Death comes equally to everyone by nature
p: Otho decides to die for something. Ecclesiastes saw the same fact and drew another lesson.
b: Otho argues that since everyone dies, a bold man should risk death for a prize. Ecclesiastes sees the same sameness of fate: "time and chance meet them all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Tacitus lets Otho's logic stand as an example of how ambition talks itself into a crime. Christians set the sameness of death beside the hope of resurrection; the site's topic on resurrection gives that.

a: The astrologers pushed him too
t: Astrologers in Rome and in the Bible
p: Rome banned astrologers and kept using them. The Bible mocks the Babylonian version.
b: The Latin is mathematici, "astrologers." Tacitus says they are a kind of man "forbidden" in Rome and always "kept." Isaiah mocks Babylon's astrologers: "the ones who map out the sky, / who stare at the stars" (Isaiah 47:13). Daniel opens with a king calling "the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers and the Chaldeans" (Daniel 2:2). The magi of Matthew 2 saw "his star at its rising" (Matthew 2:2), a case where watching the sky leads to the Messiah. Link strength: real as a practice; the Bible's verdict differs in each case.

a: One of them
p: Suetonius names the astrologer Seleucus. Tacitus names Ptolemaeus.
b: Suetonius says the astrologer Seleucus told Otho he would outlive Nero and become emperor (Otho 4.1). Tacitus names the astrologer Ptolemaeus (1:22), and Thayer's note on Suetonius, Otho 4, says Tacitus and Plutarch both give Ptolemaeus (Plutarch, Galba 23). The writers tell the same prediction with different names for the man. Link strength: strong on the prediction; Tacitus and Plutarch give Ptolemaeus, Suetonius Seleucus.

a: the cities of Achaia
p: Nero toured Greece. Josephus mentions Achaia and Nero together.
b: Achaia was the Roman province of Greece. Josephus says Vespasian "sent his son Titus from Achaia, where he had been with Nero" (Jewish War 3.1.3). Acts names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia when the Jews brought Paul before him (Acts 18:12). Tacitus uses the picture of Nero's soldiers sailing to Campania's lakes and the Greek cities to show how soft they had become.

a: a hundred sesterces to every man of the cohort on guard duty
t: What a hundred sesterces is worth
p: A hundred sesterces is twenty-five denarii, twenty-five days of a laborer's pay.
b: At four sesterces to the denarius (Wikipedia, Denarius), a hundred sesterces is twenty-five denarii. In Jesus' parable a worker's day was one denarius (Matthew 20:2). So each guard on duty got about twenty-five days' wage as a free gift at dinner. Otho gave this whenever Galba dined with him. John the Baptist's rule for soldiers was the opposite: "Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14).

a: gave out the watchword to the bodyguard
p: The Latin "speculator" reached the Gospels as a Greek loanword.
b: The Latin is tesserarium speculatorum: the man who gave out the tessera, the watchword, to the speculatores. Mark uses the Latin word in Greek letters, spekoulator, for Herod's "executioner" who beheaded John (Mark 6:27). Same unit? Possible, not shown: the Gospel word names a royal guard on a task, and Tacitus's speculatores are Roman guardsmen. The shared word is the link.

a: So two common soldiers took on the job of transferring the empire of the Roman people, and they did transfer it.
t: Two soldiers and the cost of an empire
p: Claude's theory: Tacitus's sentence about two men shows how little it took.
b: My theory. The Latin is suscepere duo manipulares imperium populi Romani transferendum et transtulerunt. The paired verbs make the point: two ordinary soldiers took on the job, and the job was done. Tacitus is angry here, not neutral. Compare Daniel: "he removes kings and he sets kings up" (Daniel 2:21). Where Daniel sees God moving thrones, Tacitus sees two men and some money. A Christian can hold both: God allows (Romans 13:1) and rulers are still answerable for how they got power. A web search on 3 November 2026 found no published comparison of this sentence with Daniel 2:21, so the comparison is mine.

a: On the eighteenth day before the first of February
t: The date of the coup: 15 January
p: The eighteenth day before the Kalends of February is 15 January.
b: The Latin is Octavo decimo kalendas Februarias. The Kalends is the first of the month, and Romans counted back inclusively (Wikipedia, Roman calendar), so the eighteenth day before 1 February is 15 January. The Year of the Four Emperors page also gives 15 January for the killing of Galba and Piso.

a: the reader of entrails Umbricius
p: A haruspex read the liver. Ezekiel shows a Babylonian king doing the same.
b: Wikipedia says a haruspex inspected the entrails of sacrificed animals, especially the liver, to see whether the gods approved. Umbricius reads "gloomy" signs for Galba. Ezekiel pictures the king of Babylon at a crossroads: "He rattles the arrows. He asks questions of the teraphim. He examines the liver" (Ezekiel 21:21). Agrees: liver reading is the same practice. Differs: in Ezekiel the same omen-reading is made to serve God's judgment on Jerusalem; Deuteronomy forbids Israel to practice it (Deuteronomy 18:10).

a: the architect and the contractors were waiting for him
t: The signal in Suetonius and Plutarch
p: Suetonius and Plutarch also have a builders' signal.
b: Plutarch: Onomastus told Otho that builders were waiting, a cover for leaving (Galba 24.2-3). Suetonius: a freedman announced the architects' arrival, the agreed signal (Otho 6.2). Tacitus has the same pretext. Link strength: strong. Three writers give the same signal. They differ on small details such as the number who met Otho.

a: twenty-three bodyguards
t: How many soldiers? Tacitus, Plutarch and Suetonius
p: Tacitus and Plutarch say twenty-three. Suetonius counts fifteen conspirators.
b: Tacitus says twenty-three speculatores hailed Otho (tres et viginti). Plutarch says the soldiers who first welcomed him and saluted him as emperor "were no more than twenty-three" (Galba 25.1, Loeb, Perrin). Suetonius counts the plot differently: five bodyguards were trusted first, then ten others, two chosen by each of the first five, so fifteen (Otho 5.2), and he does not give twenty-three. Wikipedia's page on the Guard also says twenty-three. Link strength: strong for the event. The sources give 23 (Tacitus, Plutarch, Wikipedia) and 15 (Suetonius), and they do not agree. The reader sees how an empire turned on a handful.

a: the golden milestone
p: A gilded column in the Forum where, the story went, Italy's roads met.
b: Plutarch says Otho went down into the Forum "to where a gilded column stood, at which all the roads that intersect Italy terminate" (Galba 24.4, Loeb, Perrin). Suetonius names the golden mile-post near the temple of Saturn (Otho 6.2). Thayer's note on that passage describes a pillar covered with gilded bronze, put up by Augustus in 20 BC, with the names of the main cities of the empire and their distances from Rome. It adds that the roads were supposed to meet at that point, but the distances on them were reckoned from the gates.

a: The tribune on duty in the camp was Julius Martialis.
p: Plutarch names the same tribune and says he let Otho in.
b: Plutarch says soldiers kept joining Otho as he was carried through the Forum. At the camp, he says, Martialis, the military tribune in charge of the watch at the time, was not in on the plot, as they say, but was confounded and terrified by their sudden appearance and let them in (Galba 25.2-3). Tacitus says Martialis was stunned or afraid, and "made many suspect he was part of it." Link strength: strong. Both name the man and the action. Plutarch reports that he was not in the plot, as they say; Tacitus records the suspicion.

a: Piso called the soldiers together
t: Piso's speech and Paul's "good fortune" warning
p: Piso warns of the danger of good fortune. Tacitus's first speech by Piso repeats Galba's theme.
b: Piso says, "I have known bad fortune, and right now I am learning that good fortune is no less dangerous." It repeats Galba's advice at 1:15. Proverbs pictures the same danger: if you are full you may "deny you, / and say, 'Who is the LORD?'" (Proverbs 30:9). The speech is Tacitus's composition (see the note at 1:15). The twin themes show the book's moral view: success tests character more than failure does.

a: Marius Celsus was sent to the picked troops of the Illyrian army
p: Galba's officers try to hold the camps; none succeed.
b: Celsus, the consul-elect, tries the Illyrian troops and is driven away with javelins (1:31). Other officers are sent to the German detachments and the Praetorian camp. The Illyrian troops were the army of the Balkan lands; Paul had preached "as far as Illyricum" (Romans 15:19). Plutarch places Celsus and Laco among those who urged Galba to go out (Galba 26.1).

a: Titus Vinius thought he should stay inside the house
p: Plutarch says Vinius argued against leaving and Celsus and Laco argued for it.
b: Plutarch says that as Galba was about to go out, Vinius would not allow it, while Celsus and Laco urged him to go and sharply rebuked Vinius (Galba 26.1). Tacitus has Vinius for staying and "the others" for going out, with Laco attacking Vinius (1:33). Link strength: strong. The two agree on who argued which side. Plutarch also names Celsus on the side of going out.

a: Julius Atticus, who held up a bloody sword and shouted that he had killed Otho
p: Tacitus, Suetonius and Plutarch all record Galba asking the soldier who ordered it.
b: Tacitus: "Fellow soldier," Galba said, "who ordered it?" (1:35). Suetonius: a soldier boasted that he had slain Otho, and Galba asked "On whose authority?" (Galba 19.2). Plutarch: Galba asks, "Who gave thee thy orders?" (Galba 26.2). Link strength: strong. All three give the question; the exact words are each writer's own wording.

a: decimated
p: "Decimated" means one man in ten was put to death.
b: Wikipedia: decimation was a Roman military punishment in which every tenth man in a group was executed, with lots drawn and the condemned clubbed to death by their comrades. Otho says Galba did this to surrendered men who had asked for mercy. Wikipedia's decimation page says Galba decimated a unit that refused demotion to naval service; it does not mention the Mulvian Bridge. Tacitus's rumor at 1:51 that legions were being decimated shows the fear the word caused.

a: Obultronius Sabinus and Cornelius Marcellus in Spain, Betuus Chilo in Gaul, Fonteius Capito in Germany, Clodius Macer in Africa, Cingonius on the road, Turpilianus in the city, and Nymphidius in the camp
p: Otho names eight men and the places where Galba had them killed.
b: The list covers the whole empire: Spain, Gaul, Germany, Africa, the road to Rome, Rome itself and the Praetorian camp. Five of the eight are explained elsewhere in Book 1: Capito and Macer at 1:7, Cingonius and Turpilianus at 1:6, Nymphidius at 1:5. Otho is making a case, so the list is a politician's list. Tacitus gives no separate account of Obultronius Sabinus, Cornelius Marcellus or Betuus Chilo in this book.

a: the Polycleti, the Vatinii
t: Polycletus and the other rich freedmen
p: The three names stand for freedmen who grew rich under Nero.
b: The Latin has Polycliti et Vatinii et Aegiali. The Church and Brodribb English reads "the Elii" for the last; the Latin has Aegiali. Otho says Icelus has grabbed more in seven months than they wasted. A freedman rising to wealth in the emperor's household is the same world as "those who belong to Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22).

a: It's only seven months since Nero's end
p: Nero died on 9 June 68, and the speech is in mid-January 69.
b: Wikipedia dates Nero's death to 9 June 68. Seven months later is the second week of January 69, which fits the speech on 15 January. Josephus counts Galba's reign as seven months and seven days (Jewish War 4.9.2).

a: the gods showed with a notable storm that they turned away from that ill-fated adoption
p: Plutarch also reads the storm as a sign against the adoption.
b: Plutarch says the storm interrupted the address and he reads it as a sign that the adoption was not favored by the gods (Galba 23). Tacitus gives Otho the same reading in a speech to the soldiers. Link strength: strong. Otho uses a sign that Galba brushed aside at 1:18; Tacitus does not say whether he believes it.

a: Vologesus or Pacorus off the ancestral throne of the Arsacids
p: Parthia was Rome's great rival. Parthians are named at Pentecost in Acts.
b: Vologesus and Pacorus are Parthian kings of the Arsacid family. Tacitus says Otho's soldiers charged as if after a Parthian king. Acts lists Parthians first among those in Jerusalem at Pentecost: "We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites" (Acts 2:9).

a: tore down Galba's image and threw it to the ground
p: Armies carried the emperor's image. Jesus asked whose image was on the coin.
b: Wikipedia says an image-bearer carried the emperor's image from Augustus onward, and Tacitus has the standard-bearer of Galba's escort throw down Galba's image to show the troops had changed sides. Jesus asked, "Whose image is this, and whose name is written here?" and they answered, "Caesar's" (Matthew 22:20-21). Link strength: background. The image of the ruler meant his claim on those who carried it.

a: Near the Lake of Curtius
t: Where Galba died, in three writers
p: Three writers place Galba's death at the Lake of Curtius in the Forum.
b: Suetonius: he was killed in the Forum, beside the Lake of Curtius (Galba 20.2). Plutarch: the litter overturned at the Lake of Curtius (Galba 27.1). Tacitus: "Near the Lake of Curtius, Galba's bearers panicked and he was thrown out of his chair." Link strength: strong. They differ on the last words and on who struck (see the note on his last words at this verse). Josephus says only that Galba was slain "in the midst of the Roman market-place" (Jewish War 4.9.9).

a: His last words have been told differently
t: Galba's last words in three writers
p: Tacitus gives two reports of Galba's last words. Suetonius and Plutarch give others.
b: Tacitus gives two reports: a plea in a pleading voice for a few days to pay the bonus, and, as the more common one, an offered throat with the words to strike "if that seemed best for the state." Suetonius gives two as well: some say Galba cried out, "What mean you, fellow soldiers? I am yours and you are mine," and even promised largess, but "the more general account" is that he offered his neck without resistance, urging them to do their duty and strike (Galba 20.1, Loeb, Rolfe). Plutarch has him present his neck and say, "Do your work, if this is better for the Roman people" (Galba 27.1, Loeb, Perrin). Link strength: strong on the offered neck, which all three have. The plea for time to pay the bonus is Tacitus's alone; the cry to the soldiers and the promise of largess are Suetonius's alone. Each writer gives the words in his own wording. On who struck, Tacitus names Terentius, Laecanius or Camurius, and Plutarch says most writers name Camurius, with some naming Terentius, Lecanius or Fabius Fabulus (Galba 27.2).

a: he cried out that Otho had not ordered him killed
p: Plutarch has Vinius claim Otho did not want him killed.
b: Plutarch says Vinius was killed, and that he showed himself a party to the plot against Galba by crying out that he was put to death "contrary to the wishes of Otho" (Galba 27.4). Tacitus: "whether his rising fear took away his voice, or whether he cried out that Otho had not ordered him killed." Link strength: strong on the cry. Plutarch takes it as an admission that Vinius was in the plot; Tacitus says it was disputed, and that if it was made up out of fear or was a confession, Vinius was in on the crime (1:42).

a: Sempronius Densus
p: Plutarch also tells of the centurion who fought for Galba's litter.
b: Plutarch: Sempronius Densus, a centurion, defended the litter in the Forum and was wounded (Galba 26.4-5). Tacitus says he was a Praetorian centurion posted to guard Piso, that he drew his dagger on the attackers and gave Piso a chance to flee. Link strength: strong. The two place Densus in the same fight; Plutarch ties it to Galba's litter, Tacitus to Piso.

a: Piso made it to the temple of Vesta.
p: The temple did not save Piso. Moses's law said an altar could not shield a murderer.
b: Tacitus says it was "not the holiness of the place or its rites but the hiding place" that put off death, and Piso was killed in the doorway. In Israel, the horns of the altar were a place of refuge, but Moses's law says of a murderer, "take him away even from my altar to die" (Exodus 21:14). Joab seized the altar's horns and was struck down there (1 Kings 2:28-31). Plutarch says a certain Murcus ran Piso down and killed him (Galba 27.4). Link strength: shared theme of the altar as refuge.

a: He ordered all of them hunted down and killed
t: Rewarding a killer of a ruler
p: Vitellius, like David, killed men who came for a reward after a ruler's death.
b: Vitellius found over 120 petitions from people asking for a reward for a notable service on the day Galba and Piso died, and had all of them hunted down. Tacitus says it was done "not to honor Galba, but in the old custom of rulers." David did the same when men brought him Ish-bosheth's head: "Evil men have murdered a man who did nothing wrong... will I not demand his blood from your hands?" (2 Samuel 4:11). He also had a man killed who claimed to have killed Saul (2 Samuel 1:14-16). Agrees: a new ruler who rewards a murder invites the next. The reasons differ: David acts on justice, Vitellius on safety.

a: They made Flavius Sabinus prefect of the city
p: The prefect of the city was Vespasian's brother.
b: Tacitus says many looked to Vespasian in this choice, "his brother." The prefect of the city governed Rome in the emperor's absence. Tacitus tells his end in Book 3: after the fight on the Capitol he was taken to Vitellius, struck down and dragged to the Gemoniae (3:74-75). Wikipedia's page on Domitian dates this 19 December 69. This is background to the Flavians, not a Bible figure.

a: The ordinary soldier paid them like a yearly tax.
p: Soldiers paid their centurions for time off. John told soldiers not to squeeze money by force.
b: Tacitus describes a system in which a soldier paid his centurion a fee to be away from duty, and made the money by robbery or by working as a slave. John the Baptist said to soldiers, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges. Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14). Agrees: both treat extortion by soldiers as a real, common wrong. Otho's cure was to pay the fees from his own purse; Tacitus calls it "clearly a useful reform."

a: the name Augustus
p: Augustus began as a man's name and became the title of every emperor.
b: Luke's "Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1) is the first emperor. Here the Senate votes the same name as a title to Otho. The Greek form is Sebastos: the Emperor's Cohort in Acts 27:1 is the cohort "of Augustus" in the Greek (speirēs Sebastēs), and Festus says Paul appealed "for the verdict of the emperor" (Acts 25:21), where the Greek word for emperor is the same title, Sebastos. Same person? Luke's Augustus and Tacitus's divine Augustus are one man. The title passes to Otho only because the Senate says so.

a: Piso was completing his thirty-first year
p: Piso was thirty. His brothers had been killed under Claudius and Nero.
b: Tacitus gives Piso a good name and bad luck. Galba's quick adoption "gave him only this advantage over his older brother: that he died first." Plutarch says Piso's head went to his wife Verania and Vinius's to his daughter (Galba 28). Tacitus agrees at 1:47: Verania and Scribonianus buried Piso, Crispina buried Vinius.

a: in seventy-three years passed through the reigns of five emperors
p: Tacitus and Suetonius say seventy-three years. Wikipedia's birth date makes him about seventy.
b: Suetonius says Galba died "in his seventy-third year" and the seventh month of his reign (Galba 23.1). Wikipedia gives his birth as 24 December 3 BC and his reign as 8 June 68 to 15 January 69, and notes that this makes him about seventy, while Suetonius and Tacitus put him in his 73rd year, which would put the birth at 5 BC. Josephus counts seven months and seven days (Jewish War 4.9.2). The five emperors Galba lived under are Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero.

a: covered it with a humble burial in Galba's own gardens
p: Saul's body was abused and then buried by loyal men. So was Galba's.
b: Tacitus says Galba's body lay neglected and abused and was buried by his steward Argius in Galba's gardens. After Saul's death the Philistines hacked off his head and fastened his body to a wall; "Every man of courage" from Jabesh-gilead took the body down and buried the bones (1 Samuel 31:9-13). Plutarch says Galba's head was thrown at the Sessorium and Helvidius had the body buried at night by the freedman Argivus (Galba 28.2-3). Link strength: shared pattern, not a source.

a: His own talent was middling, more free of vices than full of virtues.
p: Tacitus gives Galba mixed marks.
b: The portrait mixes good and bad: noble family, middling talent, "more free of vices than full of virtues," careful with his own money and greedy with the public's. He was fair as governor of Africa and Nearer Spain. His end is summed up in the line "by everyone's agreement he would have been judged fit to rule if he had never ruled." Historical-critical view: Tacitus closes the lives of Galba, Piso and Vinius (1:48-49) and Tigellinus (1:72) with a short judgment of this kind. Christian reading: a ruler's character is measured by what he does with power, which is the Bible's test (Deuteronomy 17:14-20, see the site's topic on kingship).

a: Pharsalia, Philippi, Perusia and Mutina
t: Philippi, a battlefield and a church
p: Philippi was the site of a civil war battle. Paul planted a church there.
b: Tacitus names old civil-war battlefields. Philippi was where Octavian and Antony beat Brutus. The site's topic on Philippi says it was refounded as a Roman colony after the battle of 42 BC. Acts says of it, "one of the foremost cities of its district of Macedonia, and a colony" (Acts 16:12). Link strength: the place is the same. The Roman soldier settlers at Philippi explain why Paul's use of his citizenship there mattered (Acts 16:37).

a: Now are we to go to the temples for Otho or for Vitellius?
p: Romans despaired of praying for either emperor. Paul tells Christians to pray for all in power.
b: Tacitus says prayers for either man would be "impious" and vows "hateful." Paul wrote, "make requests, prayers, appeals and thanksgivings for every person, for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Peter wrote, "Give honor to the king" (1 Peter 2:17). Differs: the Christian prays for the ruler whether he is good or bad, so that "we can spend calm and quiet lives" (1 Timothy 2:2). The site's topic on the church and the ruler sets out the debates.

a: Some predicted Vespasian and the armies of the East
p: Tacitus knew how the year ended when he wrote this.
b: He says Vespasian was "better than either of them" and "the only emperor before himself who changed for the better." The Latin solusque omnium ante se principum in melius mutatus est is a statement written after the fact: Vespasian was proclaimed at Alexandria on 1 July (Wikipedia). Tacitus's debt to Vespasian (1:1) colors it. Josephus too sided with Vespasian after being taken at Jotapata (Wikipedia, Josephus).

a: Alienus Caecina and Fabius Valens
p: Caecina and Valens will march the armies into Italy.
b: Tacitus introduces them as legates of the legions, "overflowing" in greed and "remarkable" in recklessness. Valens pushes Vitellius to claim the throne. Wikipedia says both owed their rise to Vitellius, that Caecina later tried to defect to Vespasian, and that Valens was captured and executed by Vespasian's forces. Their march is in 1:61-70 and is told on in Books 2 and 3.

a: gifts of right hands, the sign of hospitality
p: The Lingones sent right hands as a sign of friendship. Paul received one at Jerusalem.
b: Tacitus says the Lingones sent models of clasped right hands to the legions, an old sign of hospitality. In Galatians Paul says James, Cephas and John "gave Barnabas and me their right hands in partnership" (Galatians 2:9). Link strength: background. The handshake as pledge is a common sign in many cultures.

a: called on the names of the Senate and people of Rome
p: The legions swore by the old Republic's name, not the emperor's.
b: The Latin phrase is in senatus ac populi Romani verba iurasse (1:56). It is the formula of the old Republic. Tacitus says the oath looked "empty" (1:56) and the Upper army dropped the phrase on 3 January for Vitellius (1:57). The oath was the personal bond of each soldier (sacramentum). The soldiers' oath in Book 1 shifts three times in under three weeks: to Galba, to the Senate and people, to Vitellius.
orig: in senatus ac populi Romani verba

a: eagle-bearer
p: The eagle was the legion's sacred standard; the eagle-bearer carried it.
b: The Latin is aquilifer. Wikipedia says each legion's standard was an eagle (aquila) carried by the aquilifer, that losing it was a grave disgrace, and that it could lead to a legion being broken up. The Church and Brodribb English reads "standard-bearer"; the Latin is more exact (see the variant). The eagle carried by the legion at 1:44 is the same object.

a: On the night after the first of January
p: The Rhine mutiny took three days.
b: On 1 January the oath was refused or half-taken (1:55). That night the eagle-bearer rode to Colonia Agrippinensis and told Vitellius at dinner (1:56). The next day, 2 January, Fabius Valens hailed him emperor (1:57). The Upper army joined on 3 January (1:57). Wikipedia's page on Vitellius also gives the proclamation at Cologne "the next day" after 1 January.

a: the third day before the nones of January
p: The third day before the Nones of January is 3 January.
b: The Latin is tertium nonas Ianuarias. In January the Nones fall on the 5th (Wikipedia, Roman calendar), and Romans counted inclusively, so the third day before is the 3rd. Tacitus adds that the Upper army had not really been the state's army in the two days before.

a: They handed over their travel pay, their belts, and the silver-trimmed ornaments of their weapons in place of money
p: The soldiers gave their belts and decorations for the cause.
b: The Latin is viatica sua et balteos phalerasque, insignia armorum argento decora: "their travel money, their belts and phalerae, the decorations of their arms, trimmed with silver." Tacitus says the men gave these in place of money "from impulse and passion and greed." Phalerae are named in the Latin and kept in the Conversational English Translation as "silver-trimmed ornaments of their weapons."

a: He assigned to Roman Knights the services of the emperor's household that freedmen normally carried out
p: The emperor's household was staffed by freedmen. Paul sends greetings from "Caesar's household."
b: Vitellius gave the household jobs to Roman Knights rather than freedmen, which Tacitus mentions as a gesture to old Roman feeling. Paul writes from Rome, "All the saints send you greetings, and above all those who belong to Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22). The household of Caesar included slaves and freedmen of all ranks. Link strength: the household is real. It shows why a Christian could be "in" the emperor's service without being a Knight.

a: Pompeius Propinquus, the procurator of Belgica, was killed at once.
p: Vitellius's men killed the procurator who had warned Galba.
b: Propinquus is the officer whose letter reached Galba at 1:12. Wikipedia says a procurator ran a province's finances and answered to the emperor, not to the governor. Tacitus uses him to show Vitellius's army taking revenge at once.

a: There were eight Batavian cohorts
p: The Batavians served Rome as auxiliaries, not citizen soldiers.
b: Wikipedia says auxiliaries were non-citizens who served in cohorts and cavalry wings, and, Wikipedia says, were given citizenship at the end of their service (a rule it says is deduced from the date of the first known military diplomas). The eight Batavian cohorts had been attached to the 14th legion and had split off from it. Julius Civilis, a Batavian leader, becomes important in Book 4. Tacitus introduces him here as a man pulled out of danger because the Batavians were too strong to anger.

a: he forbade being called Caesar even after his victory
p: Caesar began as a family name and became a title.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius took the name Germanicus but refused "Caesar." The Latin is Caesarem se appellari etiam victor prohibuit. Piso is called "Caesar by adoption" at 1:29. The Gospels and Acts use the title, not the family name: "pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar" (Matthew 22:21), "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11), "those who belong to Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22). Link strength: same title, different emperors.
orig: Caesarem se appellari etiam victor prohibuit

a: an eagle flew ahead of the column in a gentle glide
p: A bird in the sky was taken as a sign. The Bible forbids the practice but also uses birds as pictures.
b: Tacitus reports a lucky omen: an eagle flew ahead of the marching column like a guide. Romans read birds as the gods' signs, a craft called augury. Deuteronomy bans anyone who "practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens" (Deuteronomy 18:10). The Bible's eagle is often God's image: he says, "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me" (Exodus 19:4). Differs: a sign from God is given by God for a purpose, not read from a bird's flight.

a: They carried out veils and wool bands of suppliants
t: Suppliants in Rome and in Israel
p: The people of Vienna begged for mercy in their own sign. Ben-hadad's men did the same in 1 Kings.
b: Tacitus says the people of Vienna carried the signs of suppliants and clung to the soldiers' weapons, knees and feet. In 1 Kings, Ben-hadad's servants "tie sackcloth on our waists and put ropes on our heads" and go to the king of Israel to ask that Ben-hadad's life be spared (1 Kings 20:31-32). Agrees: a public sign of surrender asked for mercy in both. The result differs: Vienna was fined; Ben-hadad was called "my brother."

a: many thousands were sold into slavery
p: Selling the defeated was normal in Roman war.
b: Tacitus says that after Caecina's victory many thousands of the Helvetii were killed and many thousands sold. The Bible's Israel knew captives as spoil (Deuteronomy 20:14), and Josephus reports that after the fall of Jerusalem those under seventeen years of age were sold as slaves (Jewish War 6.9.2). The site's topic on slavery covers how the Bible treats it.

a: Mediolanum, Novaria, Eporedia and Vercellae
p: The first towns of north Italy went over to Vitellius without a fight.
b: A cavalry wing that had once served under Vitellius in Africa swore to him around the Padus (the Po) and gave him these four towns as a gift. The towns are on the route from the Alps into the Italian plain. They give Caecina a foothold before he has crossed the mountains.

a: stained his infamous life further with a late and dishonorable death
p: Tigellinus ended his own life; the Bible tells of few such deaths.
b: Tigellinus had held command of the watch and of the Praetorian Guard under Nero (1:72). Tacitus tells his death briefly: he heard that his last hour had come and ended his own life. The Bible tells of Saul, who fell on his sword (1 Samuel 31:4), and Judas, who "went off. Then he went and hanged himself" (Matthew 27:5). The site's topic on suicide covers how the churches have judged such deaths. Tacitus's own word is "dishonorable." Otho also ends his own life after Bedriacum (Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.9; Suetonius, Otho 11).

a: to bring famine on the Roman people
t: Famine as a weapon, and Acts 11:28
p: Calvia Crispinilla is accused of starving Rome. Acts and Josephus tell of a real famine under Claudius.
b: Tacitus says Crispinilla crossed to Africa to push Clodius Macer to revolt, and that she plotted openly to bring famine on the Roman people. Acts says a great famine struck "the whole inhabited world... in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28). Josephus says the great famine fell in Judea under the procurators Fadus and Tiberius Alexander, when Queen Helena bought corn in Egypt (Antiquities 20.5.2). Link strength: Acts and Josephus agree on a famine in the reign of Claudius; Tacitus's famine is a plot, not that event.

a: Vitellius wrote to Titianus, Otho's brother
p: Each emperor held the other's family hostage in words, and neither carried out the threat.
b: Vitellius threatens death to Titianus and his son unless Vitellius's mother and children are kept safe. Neither side hurt the other's family. Tacitus says Otho may have spared them out of fear, but Vitellius "got the glory of mercy." Salvius Titianus is the brother Otho leaves in charge of Rome (1:90).

a: Vespasian had the army in Judea and Mucianus the legions in Syria swear Otho's oath
p: Tacitus has the army of Judea swear Otho's oath. The pause in the war is Josephus's.
b: Tacitus: Vespasian and Mucianus had their armies take the oath to Otho. Josephus: Vespasian "put off at first his expedition against Jerusalem, and stood waiting whither the empire would be transferred" (Jewish War 4.9.2). The oath is Tacitus's; the pause is Josephus's, and Tacitus does not state it in Book 1. Link strength: the oath is Tacitus's; the pause comes from Josephus.
