Many Christians read Luke 21:20-24 of the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70, and these are the months before it.

a: Egypt and all the provinces facing the East were held in his name
p: The East held for Otho through Egypt's prefect.
b: Egypt's prefect was Tiberius Alexander (1:11). Later he had the legions at Alexandria swear to Vespasian on 1 July 69 (Tacitus 2:79; Josephus, Jewish War 4.10.6). Syria, Judea, Egypt and the other eastern provinces held their oaths to Otho until Vespasian was proclaimed. Africa swore at Carthage (1:76).

a: legions of Dalmatia, Pannonia and Moesia
p: The Bible names Dalmatia once, in 2 Timothy. A freedman named Crescens appears in the same verse of Tacitus.
b: Dalmatia is the Roman province on the Adriatic coast of the Balkans, whose legions swore to Otho. The Bible names it once: "Crescens went to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia" (2 Timothy 4:10). The site's variant at that verse records that Codex Sinaiticus reads "Gaul" for "Galatia." Tacitus's Gauls (1:2, 1:8) and Narbonensis, which turns to Vitellius in this verse, are the western land that reading would mean. No link: the freedman Crescens who gives a banquet at Carthage later in 1:76 shares only a name with the Crescens of 2 Timothy 4:10. Nothing ties them together.

a: He made himself consul with his brother Titianus until the first of March
p: Consuls resigned partway through the year so more men could hold the office.
b: Wikipedia says that in the empire ordinary consuls often resigned partway through the year, and that Augustus reworked the office of substitute consul so more than two could serve in a year. Otho takes the first two months for himself and his brother, sets the next months for Verginius and Pompeius Vopiscus, then Caelius and Flavius Sabinus until 1 July, and Arrius Antoninus and Marius Celsus until September. The year's name stayed Galba and Vinius, but the real consuls kept changing.

a: gave Roman citizenship to all the Lingones
p: Otho gave a whole people the Roman franchise. Paul's citizenship was either inherited or bought.
b: The Lingones were a Gallic people who had hosted the legions and now helped Vitellius (1:54, 1:57). Otho's grant to them is a bid for loyalty. In Acts, the Roman citizenship is never given to a whole people: Paul's came by birth, the commander's by purchase (Acts 22:28). Differs: Otho's gift is political and sudden; Paul's is personal and legal.

a: He gave Cappadocia new rights
p: Cappadocia is named at Pentecost and in 1 Peter.
b: Cappadocia was a Roman province in Asia Minor. Acts lists Cappadocia among the homelands of those in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). Peter's first letter is addressed to believers "in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1). Link strength: place only. Tacitus names Otho's gifts to provinces that were not his to give for long.

a: shouted to Otho "Nero Otho,"
p: Suetonius also says the crowd called Otho Nero, and that he did not object.
b: Suetonius: Otho was called "Nero" by the crowd and reportedly did not object. He restored Nero's busts and statues and reinstated Nero's procurators and freedmen (Otho 7.1). Tacitus says Otho "left it hanging, afraid to forbid it or ashamed to accept it." Link strength: strong. Suetonius goes further than Tacitus: he says Otho restored Nero's statues and officials; Tacitus says only that Otho put back Poppaea's statues and was believed to have thought about honoring Nero's memory. The site's note on Revelation 13:3 gives the Nero legend that grew after his death.

a: a Sarmatae people
p: The Roxolani were horsemen of the Sarmatae.
b: The Latin is Rhoxolani in Fisher's text; the English spells it Roxolani. The Sarmatae were a horse-riding people. Tacitus describes their heavy armor and long swords, and how both failed in a thaw. The Roman victory is told in the same verse. They are not named in the Bible.

a: Marcus Aponius, who held Moesia, was given a triumphal statue
p: The Senate gave honors to the commanders. Otho took the credit.
b: A triumphal statue and "the honors of consuls" were rewards the Senate could give without a full triumph. Tacitus says Otho "drew the glory to himself." The Senate here acts as the giver of honors even in a year when it has no real power over armies (1:47; 1:85).

a: Otho had ordered the 17th cohort brought into Rome from the colony of Ostia
p: An orderly move of troops at night set off a riot.
b: Tacitus tells how the tribune Varius Crispinus loaded wagons with weapons at nightfall to spare the camp noise, and the soldiers took it for treason. In Acts, a similar mob in Jerusalem was quieted when "the commander of the cohort" came down with soldiers and centurions (Acts 21:31-32). Link strength: background only, on how Roman soldiers handled crowds. Wikipedia says the urban cohorts were numbered after the praetorian cohorts; Tacitus does not say which kind this was.

a: 5,000 sesterces being paid to each soldier
p: Otho paid each soldier 5,000 sesterces to end the riot.
b: At four sesterces to the denarius (Wikipedia, Denarius), that is 1,250 denarii each. In Jesus' parable a worker's day was a denarius (Matthew 20:2), so the payment equals 1,250 days of a laborer's wage. Tacitus does not say how much the gift was worth in his day. It shows that even a riot against the Senate ended with a bonus.

a: If each man may ask why he is being ordered, obedience dies, and command with it.
p: Otho's rule of obedience is the centurion's rule in Luke.
b: Otho says an army is held together by obeying, not by questioning orders (1:84). A centurion told Jesus, "I am a man placed under someone's authority myself, and I have soldiers under me. I say 'Go!' to this one, and off he goes" (Luke 7:8). Jesus "was amazed at him" and said, "I have not met faith this great even in Israel" (Luke 7:9). Another centurion, Cornelius, served "in the unit called the Italian Cohort" (Acts 10:1). Agrees: both describe command as a chain. The Gospel uses that chain as a picture of faith in Jesus's word; Otho uses it to excuse the Guard's riot.

a: Omens, reported by different sources, added to the terror.
p: Tacitus lists prodigies. Jesus spoke of signs and a roaring sea.
b: A chariot's reins slipped from the statue of Victory, a form larger than a human burst out of Juno's shrine, a statue turned on a clear day, an ox spoke in Etruria. Jesus: "there will be signs in the sun, the moon and the stars. On the earth the nations will be gripped with dread, not knowing where to turn at the roar of the sea and the heaving waves" (Luke 21:25). A speaking animal also appears in Numbers: "Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, 'What have I done to you, that you have beaten me these three times?'" (Numbers 22:28). Differs: in Numbers the story says the LORD opened the donkey's mouth; Tacitus lists the ox's speech among reports read as warnings. Link strength: a parallel and a likeness in mood, not a source. Suetonius says Otho ignored unfavorable omens when he pressed for battle (Otho 8.3, 9.1).

a: a sudden flood of the Tiber
p: The flood brought hunger. Tacitus lets the omen and the damage meet.
b: The river broke the wooden bridge and filled low parts of Rome and then others. Hunger came to the poor because there was no work and food was scarce. The flood blocked the Campus Martius and the Flaminian Way, Otho's road to the war, which people read as a sign. Jesus counts famines among the signs: "There will be famines and earthquakes in place after place" (Matthew 24:7).

a: former chief centurions
p: Primus pilus was the top centurion of a legion.
b: The Latin is primipilaribus: men who had held the post of primus pilus, the senior-most centurion, commanding the first century of the first cohort (Wikipedia). The Church and Brodribb English reads "centurions of the first rank." The Conversational English Translation at 1:31 uses the same phrase for Amullius Serenus and Domitius Sabinus.

a: Since the divine Augustus built up the power of the Caesars, the wars of the Roman people had been fought far away
t: The long peace and the Gospels
p: Tacitus says Rome's wars were far away for a century. The Gospels were set in that peace.
b: Tacitus says that from Augustus until Nero the people of Rome did not fight at home. Luke begins with a decree from Augustus (Luke 2:1). Jesus warned: "When you hear of wars and uprisings, do not be terrified. These things have to happen first, but the end will not come right away" (Luke 21:9). Link strength: background. The year 69 is the first time since the Gospel years that civil war came close to Rome. Acts 28 ends with Paul preaching "with complete freedom" in that Rome.

a: the sacred shields had not yet been put back in their place
p: A religious scruple delayed Otho; he brushed it aside.
b: The Latin is nondum conditorum ancilium: the ancient ceremonial shields had not yet been put away. Suetonius says they "had been taken out, but not yet put back," which had long been counted unlucky (Otho 8.3). Some urged Otho to wait. Tacitus says Otho "rejected every delay as having been fatal to Nero too." Suetonius says Otho ignored unfavorable omens (Otho 8.3, 9.1).

a: On March 14
t: The date: the day before the Ides of March
p: "The day before the Ides of March" is 14 March.
b: The Latin is Pridie idus Martias. In March the Ides fall on the 15th (Wikipedia, Roman calendar), so the day before is the 14th. Otho left Rome on that day; Tacitus's Book 1 ends with his departure.

a: the writer of the speech, afraid for himself
p: Tacitus says Otho may have used a speechwriter, Galerius Trachalus.
b: Tacitus says Otho was believed to use the talent of Galerius Trachalus "in city business," as he used Suetonius Paullinus and Marius Celsus in war. He adds that some knew the speaking style from Trachalus's pleading in court. The point matters for how to read speeches in the Histories: even in the real world they were often written by someone else. When Tacitus writes the speeches in Book 1 (1:15, 1:29, 1:37, 1:83) he is doing the same job in print.

a: not from fear or love but from a sheer love of servitude
p: Tacitus's "love of servitude" is the Bible's picture of the people who want a master.
b: The Latin is ex libidine servitii, "from desire for slavery." He closes the book with the crowd's flattery and ends where he began, with flattery as the enemy of truth (1:1). Israel's elders once asked Samuel for a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:5; see the site's topic on kingship); in the New Testament, believers are told, "You received the Spirit of adoption as children," not "a spirit that makes you slaves again" (Romans 8:15). Link strength: a thematic echo.
